title: Firefighter II
summary: Coordinated company operations: ventilation decisions, extrication support, foam, preplanning, radio reports, and evidence-aware overhaul.

skills.title: Coordinated Ventilation
skills.summary: Choose opening location and timing with suppression and search — not as a separate sport.
skills.whyItMatters: Firefighter II is where you stop ‘taking the roof because we always do’ and start making the fire behave on purpose.
learningPoints: State the exhaust, the inlet, and who is in the flow path before you cut or break.
Changing conditions can make yesterday’s good hole today’s blowtorch.
PPV/PPA is a coordinated tactic with rules, not a default.
Vertical ventilation needs a sound roof, staffing, and an objective.
beforeYouDo: Fire location, attack progress, search status.

terminology.meaning: The opening happens when the line and search can use the change.
Inlet to exhaust route for air and fire gases.

safetyNotes: Uncoordinated vertical vent can pull fire through crews.
Saw work on a roof is a fall/collapse problem first.

drill.objective: Given changing fire conditions, coordinate ventilation timing, location, and assignments with suppression and search.
drill.equipment: Scenario images, radios, charged line or tabletop, ventilation tools as assigned.
drill.setup: Tabletop or tower. No freelance openings.
drill.disclaimer: Completing this drill does not satisfy an official certification task, skill sheet, or Roadmap Taskbook item.

5.title: 5-minute review
5.instructions: From one photo, name inlet, intended exhaust, and who must be ready.
debrief: Who can stop the cut?

15.title: 15-minute decision set
15.instructions: Three evolving cards: kitchen fire with search, basement, and a wind-driven hint. Pick openings and timing.
debrief: What smoke change confirms it worked?

30.title: 30-minute company drill
30.instructions: Line in place, search assigned, then a ventilation order. Inject ‘too early’ and ‘wrong side.’
debrief: Did we help the search or the fire?

readinessQuestions.q: The difference between FF I support vent and FF II coordinated vent is mainly:
choices: Owning the decision of whether, where, and when with the rest of the incident

readinessQuestions.q: If search is in the planned exhaust path, you should:
choices: Change the plan — do not push fire over people

readinessQuestions.q: PPV without a coordinated exhaust and a charged line:
choices: Can push fire and products into unburned spaces and people
readinessQuestions.why: Fans change flow path on purpose — or by accident.

skills.title: Vehicle Extrication Support
skills.summary: Stabilize, create a work plan, and support patient access with approved tools — without becoming a victim of traffic or energy.
skills.whyItMatters: Cars store energy. Traffic keeps moving. The patient is not helped by a rushed, unstabilized cut.
learningPoints: Scene size-up: traffic, fuel, hybrid/EV, airbags, occupants.
Stabilize before you cut, when that is the plan.
Tool staging and roles beat a pile of iron at the C-post.
Know operations-level limits vs technician rescue.
beforeYouDo: Department vehicle-rescue SOP and the tools on YOUR rig.

terminology.meaning: Making the vehicle’s movement predictable before interior work.
Common stabilization methods — use what you carry and are trained on.

safetyNotes: Traffic is the killer on many ‘simple’ wrecks.
Undeployed airbags and high-voltage systems are not guesses — follow current department/EV guidance.
Never crawl under an unstabilized vehicle.

drill.objective: Size up a vehicle scenario, stabilize, stage tools, assign roles, and verbalize the access plan before any tool operation.
drill.equipment: Approved vehicle prop or tabletop car, rescue tools as authorized, traffic vests, cribbing/struts as carried.
drill.setup: No live traffic. Instructor controls tool use.
drill.disclaimer: Completing this drill does not satisfy an official certification task, skill sheet, or Roadmap Taskbook item.

5.title: 5-minute review
5.instructions: From a wreck photo: traffic plan, energy sources, and first stabilization idea.
debrief: Where is the safest approach?

15.title: 15-minute stabilize + stage
15.instructions: Crib/strut as trained, tool dump organized, roles assigned.
debrief: Is the vehicle done moving?

30.title: 30-minute access plan
30.instructions: Full talk-through of glass, doors, and a plan B. Include EV/hybrid inject if relevant to your response area.
debrief: When do we call a tech team?

readinessQuestions.q: Before operating hydraulic tools you should generally:
choices: Control traffic, size up energy, and stabilize per the plan
Remove your helmet to see better

readinessQuestions.q: Hybrid/EV vehicles:
choices: Can be treated exactly like 1998 Civics
Need current department/manufacturer guidance for power-down and extra hazards

readinessQuestions.q: If the rescue exceeds FF II operations-level training:
choices: Request the appropriate technical resource and protect the scene

skills.title: Foam Operations
skills.summary: Match foam to the fuel, set up proportioning equipment correctly, and know when foam is the wrong tool.
skills.whyItMatters: Wrong foam, wrong percentage, or a starved eductor wastes concentrate and fails to extinguish.
learningPoints: Fuel and foam type must match. Follow current department product guidance — formulations change.
Eductors have flow, hose-length, and nozzle constraints.
Finished-foam application is a blanket, not a stirring rod.
Environmental and runoff concerns are part of the decision.
beforeYouDo: What concentrate is on YOUR engine and what it is for.

terminology.meaning: Mixing concentrate and water at the intended percentage.
A common device that pulls concentrate using water flow — picky about setup.

safetyNotes: Flammable-liquid fire is a specialized problem. Do not treat it like a dumpster.
Runoff can spread product. Think containment.

practiceResources.label: Spill Volume Calculator
practiceResources.note: How much product might you be looking at?

drill.objective: Select foam for a stated fuel, assemble the department foam appliance correctly, and explain application and limitations.
drill.equipment: Department foam equipment, water if authorized, SDS/product sheet, radios.
drill.setup: Do not discharge foam into storm drains. Dry setup is acceptable.
drill.disclaimer: Completing this drill does not satisfy an official certification task, skill sheet, or Roadmap Taskbook item.

5.title: 5-minute review
5.instructions: Match two fuels to foam type/percentage per your product sheet.
debrief: What does the label actually say?

15.title: 15-minute setup
15.instructions: Build eductor/nozzle layout, check flow arrow, hose lengths, and pickup tube.
commonMistakes: Hose too long for the eductor
debrief: What pressure at the eductor?

30.title: 30-minute scenario
30.instructions: Small spill fire tabletop: water first? isolation? foam? runoff? When to stop.
debrief: When is this a HazMat problem, not a foam trick?

readinessQuestions.q: An eductor that does not pick up concentrate is often caused by:
choices: Wrong flow, too much hose, kink, or a closed tube

readinessQuestions.q: Foam application on a spill should generally:
choices: Blast a hole in the middle
Build a blanket gently per training — do not churn the fuel
Use a straight stream from 3 feet
Always mix Class A and B in one pail
readinessQuestions.why: Do not stir the flammable liquid.

readinessQuestions.q: FireOpsSim foam calculators are:
choices: Training estimates — confirm with the actual eductor/nozzle pair and SOP

officialSources.label: Foam concentrate and eductor manufacturer instructions
officialSources.scope: Percentages, environmental rules, and compatible hardware are product-specific.

skills.title: Preincident Survey
skills.summary: Collect the information a company will wish it had at 2 a.m.: access, water, occupancy, systems, and special hazards.
skills.whyItMatters: First-due knowledge is a firefighting skill. Guessing a building in smoke is how people get trapped.
learningPoints: Walk the occupancy with a purpose: access, forcible entry, water, utilities, fire protection, people.
Write what later crews can use — not a novel.
Note what you could not determine.
Preplans go stale. Date them.

terminology.meaning: An occupancy whose risk, complexity, or consequence deserves extra study.
Fire department connection for sprinkler/standpipe — location and condition matter.

safetyNotes: You are a guest. Do not create a tactical secret that the occupant should have told the AHJ.
Do not enter hazardous process areas beyond your training.

drill.objective: Complete a rapid preplan of an assigned occupancy covering access, water, hazards, systems, and information gaps.
drill.equipment: Local occupancy or photos, preplan form, radio optional.
drill.disclaimer: Completing this drill does not satisfy an official certification task, skill sheet, or Roadmap Taskbook item.

5.title: 5-minute review
5.instructions: List the eight things you must know about your first-due big box.
debrief: Where is the FDC?

15.title: 15-minute walk
15.instructions: Fill the FireOpsSim preplan builder or department form for one building.
debrief: What would we do at 0200 in smoke?

30.title: 30-minute company preplan
30.instructions: Whole crew walk, assignments (water, rear access, utilities), then a 2-minute arrival report from the notes.
commonMistakes: One person did it all silently
debrief: What did we still not know?

readinessQuestions.q: A useful preplan always includes:
choices: Access, water, occupancy/hazard, systems, and what is still unknown
A guarantee the building will never change

readinessQuestions.q: Hydrants and FDCs near a target occupancy:
choices: Should be verified — out-of-service and blocked connections are common
Never matter if you have a tank

readinessQuestions.q: Preplans should be:
choices: Reviewed and dated because occupancies change
Classified so the next shift cannot see them

skills.title: Company-Level Tactics
skills.summary: Turn an incident objective into firefighter tasks, benchmarks, and a radio update without pretending to be command.
skills.whyItMatters: Firefighter II is the working supervisor of a task — not the IC, not a freelancer.
learningPoints: Repeat the assignment in your own words.
Name the benchmark that means you succeeded or failed.
Call for help early when the task is bigger than the staffing.
Stay inside the role: you can recommend; the IC decides strategy.
beforeYouDo: A simple fire or rescue problem.
ICS language your department actually uses.

terminology.meaning: An observable condition that shows progress (water on fire, primary complete, utilities controlled).
You own the task; command owns the overall plan.

safetyNotes: Do not freelance a second strategy on the D side.
If you see a life hazard command missed, say it — that is not freelancing, that is communication.

seeResources.label: Fireground Decision Sim
seeResources.note: Company-level decisions inside a bigger plan.

practiceResources.label: Company Officer Tools
practiceResources.note: How officers think about your assignment.

drill.objective: Receive an assignment, restate it, execute a tabletop or practical task, and give a progress report with a benchmark.
drill.equipment: Scenario cards, radios, optional hose/ladder for a practical piece.
drill.setup: One person plays IC. Keep the FF II inside the assignment.
drill.disclaimer: Completing this drill does not satisfy an official certification task, skill sheet, or Roadmap Taskbook item.

5.title: 5-minute review
5.instructions: Practice restating: ‘You want us to… benchmark is…’
debrief: What is the benchmark for primary search?

15.title: 15-minute tabletop
15.instructions: Three assignments: backup line, utilities, and a vent group. Give updates.
debrief: When do we tell IC we cannot do it?

30.title: 30-minute evolution
30.instructions: Combined: stretch, search support, and a condition-change card. Stay in role.
debrief: Did IC actually know our progress?

readinessQuestions.q: If an assignment is bigger than your crew, you should:
choices: Tell command what you can do and what you need
Take a second company without telling anyone

readinessQuestions.q: A benchmark is useful because:
choices: It tells command whether the objective is actually happening
readinessQuestions.why: ‘Working on it’ is not a benchmark.

readinessQuestions.q: Seeing a serious unseen hazard as the assigned crew means:
choices: Stay silent to avoid bothering IC
Report it — that is part of operations

skills.title: Condition and Progress Reports
skills.summary: Give short CAN-style updates: conditions, actions, needs — so command can think.
skills.whyItMatters: Long stories clog the channel. Missing stories leave people in danger.
learningPoints: Conditions: what is the fire/building/people doing now?
Actions: what are YOU doing?
Needs: what must happen next?
If nothing changed, a short ‘unchanged’ can still be useful when asked.

terminology.meaning: Conditions, Actions, Needs — a common training structure, not a law.

safetyNotes: Do not bury a Mayday inside a casual update.
If you are in trouble, use the emergency format.

practiceResources.label: Fire Officer I — initial radio report

drill.objective: Deliver timed CAN reports from changing fireground assignments.
drill.equipment: Radio or timer, scenario cards, photos.
drill.disclaimer: Completing this drill does not satisfy an official certification task, skill sheet, or Roadmap Taskbook item.

5.title: 5-minute review
debrief: What is the need?

15.title: 15-minute reps
15.instructions: Six cards, 20 seconds each. Partner scores missing pieces.
debrief: Would IC know to send a second line?

30.title: 30-minute evolving fire
30.instructions: A scenario with three condition changes. Reports at each change.
debrief: When should this have been a Mayday instead?

readinessQuestions.q: ‘Needs’ in a progress report should be:
choices: The next resource or action required for the assignment

readinessQuestions.q: If conditions deteriorate rapidly, your radio should:
choices: Match the urgency — including emergency traffic/Mayday if that is the truth

readinessQuestions.q: CAN is:
choices: A training pattern to keep reports complete and short
readinessQuestions.why: Departments may use a different acronym. The idea is completeness.

officialSources.label: National Fire Academy
officialSources.scope: Free federal fire-service training and professional development

officialSources.label: Department radio SOP
officialSources.scope: Report format and channel use are local.

skills.title: Evidence-Aware Overhaul
skills.summary: Expose hidden fire while disturbing origin indicators as little as the fire problem allows.
skills.whyItMatters: The investigation is often won or lost by the first companies with pike poles.
learningPoints: Knock down hidden fire. That still comes first for life safety.
Do not shovel the origin out the window.
Photograph or report unusual things before they vanish if policy allows.
Chain of custody and legal rules are local — do not play detective beyond your role.

terminology.meaning: Where the fire is believed to have started — extra care.
A burn pattern or object that might help investigators — not proof by itself.

safetyNotes: Overhaul injuries and respiratory exposure are still the job hazard.

drill.objective: From scene photos, choose overhaul actions that find hidden fire and protect likely origin indicators.
drill.equipment: Scene photos, salvage cover, pike pole (optional), note sheet.
drill.setup: Tabletop is enough. Mark ‘do not toss’ items.
drill.disclaimer: Completing this drill does not satisfy an official certification task, skill sheet, or Roadmap Taskbook item.

5.title: 5-minute review
5.instructions: Name three things firefighters accidentally destroy.
debrief: Who do we notify?

15.title: 15-minute photo set
15.instructions: Five photos: room-and-contents vs suspicious vs clearly accidental. Plan overhaul depth.
debrief: What would you tell an investigator?

30.title: 30-minute practical
30.instructions: Overhaul a training room with planted ‘evidence’ and a hidden smolder sim (or card). Find the fire, leave the clue.
debrief: Did we stay on air?

readinessQuestions.q: If life safety and hidden fire conflict with preserving a room:
choices: Preserve the room and let it rekindle
Life safety and extinguishment win — then protect what is left
Remove SCBA to smell for accelerants
readinessQuestions.why: People and rekindle first, then the scene.

readinessQuestions.q: Unusual containers, pour patterns you think you see, or multiple starts:
choices: Should be reported through the department investigation path — not diagnosed as a hobby
Mean you should interrogate the occupant
readinessQuestions.why: Stay in your lane; still speak up.

readinessQuestions.q: Taking a burned object home:
choices: Is fine if it is small
readinessQuestions.why: It can be evidence. It is not yours.

officialSources.scope: Free federal fire-service training and professional development

officialSources.label: Department fire-investigation / overhaul SOP
officialSources.scope: Who investigates and how scenes are held are local and legal issues.

skills.title: Hose and Equipment Service Testing
skills.summary: Plan a safe hose/equipment service test: zones, documentation, failure criteria, and tagging out failures.
skills.whyItMatters: Burst hose on the fireground is a predictable maintenance failure. Testing is how you find it in the lot.
learningPoints: Follow current department and manufacturer test pressures — FireOpsSim will not quote a standard as if it were the law.
Safety zone: a pressurized hose is a weapon.
Document pass/fail and remove failures from service.
Testing is not a pump-operator ego contest.
beforeYouDo: Department hose-test SOP and the form.
Who may operate the test pump/gate.

terminology.meaning: A scheduled pressure/function test of hose or equipment per AHJ procedure.
The hose/device may not go back on the rig.

safetyNotes: Nobody stands over hose under test.
Hearing and eye protection as required.

drill.objective: Walk through a department hose-test workflow: layout, safety zone, documentation, and failure handling — without inventing test pressures.
drill.equipment: Department test records, cones for a safety zone, sample hose if authorized.
drill.setup: Do not pressurize hose unless a qualified instructor is running a real test.
drill.disclaimer: Completing this drill does not satisfy an official certification task, skill sheet, or Roadmap Taskbook item.

5.title: 5-minute review
5.instructions: Draw the safety zone and the ‘no-go’ line for people.
debrief: Who records pass/fail?

15.title: 15-minute paper drill
15.instructions: Fill a mock record for 10 sections. Two fail. Tag and separate them.
commonMistakes: Putting failed hose back on the bed ‘until next week’
debrief: Where does failed hose live?

30.title: 30-minute test-day plan
30.instructions: Build a full evolution with the drill builder: staffing, water source, sequence, rehab, and emergency if a line bursts.
commonMistakes: Rushing to finish before shift change
debrief: What is our burst-hose action?

readinessQuestions.q: Test pressures and intervals should come from:
Failed hose should be:
choices: Repaired with electrical tape for one more fire
readinessQuestions.why: A known failure belongs off the rig.

readinessQuestions.q: People during a hose test should be:
choices: Outside the safety zone except as the procedure requires
Using the hose as a bench
